item.content:encoded:
Akash (@Akasheth_)

Boris Cherny, the creator of claude code at anthropic, just explained why the future of AI isn't better prompts or smarter single agents.

It's teams of agents working together.

In this talk, he breaks down:

> why you're already losing context before you even start

> why one agent should research while another builds and another reviews

> the architecture serious builders are moving toward

> the core principles that make agent teams actually work

most people are still sitting in one chat window asking one agent to do everything.

meanwhile, the people building the next generation of AI products are learning how to coordinate teams of agents.

If you've been using claude, this is worth watching.

The full guide is in the article below.

Earlier, building and setting up AI agents was complex. You had to understand libraries like LangChain, set up custom Docker containers, and manage sessions, knowledge evals, and a lot of other moving parts. It was an infrastructure nightmare.
Anthropic has since launched
[Managed Agents](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/overview)
, which makes building and deploying agents much simpler than before. Within 30 minutes, I built an autonomous agent that queries my Supabase database, recommends tools, and runs in its own secure sandbox. The infrastructure management completely vanished.
If you’re still building custom harnesses for your AI agents or trying to make chatbots do agentic work, this tutorial is for you. I’m going to walk you through exactly how I built “The Tool Nerd Advisor” from scratch using Claude Managed Agents.
##
AI Agent vs Chatbot: Understanding the Difference
Every time someone says “I built an AI agent,” they usually mean they built a chatbot with a fancy system prompt. That distinction matters a lot.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKNcmngWkAA0VPn?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2063582854215266304/atrekovas/article/2063602634854982113/media/2063594872775282688)
A chatbot responds to your message and forgets everything the moment the conversation ends. It has no tools, no memory, and no ability to work independently. You have to drive every single step.
A claude-managed agent works differently at a structural level. It runs in a hosted environment, calls real APIs, executes code, and maintains state across multiple sessions. You can start a task, close your laptop, and the agent keeps working. When you come back, the full execution history is waiting for you.
Anthropic’s platform makes this possible by splitting the AI agent architecture into three separate concerns:
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKNdJFPWMAAkLnO?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2063582854215266304/atrekovas/article/2063602634854982113/media/2063595464872570880)
The Brain is the Claude model plus the harness - the system prompt, decision logic, and tool routing.
The Hands are the execution environment - a secure cloud sandbox where the agent runs code and calls APIs.
The Session is the persistent event log - an append-only record of everything that happened, which survives container restarts and context window limits.
This separation is what makes long-running AI agents possible. The container can crash, the context window can fill, and the session state still lives. You just spin up a fresh container and pick up exactly where you left off.
##
When to Deploy AI Agents in the Cloud
The question I get most often is: “When should I use a managed agent instead of just calling the LLM API directly?”
The answer comes down to three things: task duration, tool complexity, and credential security.
##
When to Use a Claude-Managed Agent vs a Chatbot
| AI Use Case | Standard Chatbot | Claude-Managed Agent |
| ------------------------------------- | ---------------- | -------------------- |
| Answer a question

There's a shift that happened around April this year that almost everyone teaching AI skills missed.
For two years, the gap between AI freelancers was skill. Who could prompt better, who knew more frameworks, who could build more Skills.
That gap closed in 2026\. Sub-agents, longer context, native Office work, scheduled Routines. The tools got good enough that pure skill stopped being scarce.
The new gap is brief quality. The senior tier figured this out in May. The tutorial industry is still teaching prompting.
Here's the shift, what a real brief looks like, and the move that puts you on the right side of it.
##
The Bar Moved When Sub-Agents Got Real
Through 2025, the senior AI builder advantage was "I can run one model very well." That advantage closed when Dynamic Workflows shipped on May 28.
One Claude session can now plan a job, spawn 200 sub-agents, and verify outputs. The execution stopped being the moat.
What's left is brief design. The person writing the job description for the swarm is the person doing the work. Everyone downstream is just running it.
The tools didn't change the deliverable. They changed where the actual work lives.
##
What A Real Brief Actually Is
A brief is not a prompt. It's not 200 words of instructions either.
A real brief has four components:
A scoped job. The thing being done is small enough that one swarm can finish it. Not "redesign our entire marketing system." More like "produce a 1-page voice-matched brief for these 15 client industries this week."
A success criterion. One sentence describing what correct output looks like. Without this, the swarm spawns and produces 200 versions of "fine."
A verification plan. How the outputs get checked without you reading every one. Usually a critic sub-agent with its own prompt.
A failure mode list. What you do when the swarm produces 12 bad outputs. The brief tells the orchestrator how to handle them.
Most people sit down to write a brief and produce a paragraph. Then they wonder why the swarm output is incoherent.
##
Where The Tutorial Industry Got Stuck
The tutorial industry is still teaching what worked in 2024\. Prompt engineering courses. Skill libraries. "10 Claude prompts that print money."
None of those move the new bar. A senior builder doesn't need 200 prompts. They need one brief that runs 200 sub-agents.
The people running tutorial channels haven't ported their lesson plans to the new shape. Their incentive is to keep selling the old curriculum. The market is paying for it because the market is still 12 months behind.
The lag between what's taught and what's paid for is now measured in skill tiers.
##
What To Do With This Right Now
The next move is small. Pick one job you'd normally hand off. Write the brief for it like you're handing it to a swarm. Watch what falls out.
The scoped job will probably be wrong on the first pass. Too big. Too vague. Cut it. Try again.
The success criterion will be obvious in hindsight and missing in the first draft. Write the line a critic sub-agent would check against.
The verification plan is the part most people skip. Write the

these seven principles are behind every single cold email campaign i've ever run. 1,800+ calls booked...
##
1\. niche down until the offer feels obvious
most people try to sell to everyone and end up resonating with nobody.
if you're an seo agency messaging "business owners who want more traffic" you're competing with 10,000 other agencies saying the exact same thing in the same inbox
niche down until your offer is so SPECIFIC that the prospect reads it and thinks "this lad is talking directly to me."
you need the 1% of your market who have the problem right now and have the budget to fix it.
if you can't describe your ideal client in one sentence with specifics (industry, company size, role, pain point), your targeting is too broad and your reply rates will reflect it
##
2\. volume is always the answer
this is the one that people push back on the most and i genuinely don't care.
i've booked 1,800+ sales calls and every single spike in results came from increasing volume.
every single dip came from decreasing it
200 emails a day is a hobby.
you'll book maybe 1-2 calls per week and spend the rest of your time wondering what's wrong with your copy.
1,000 a day is where things start to feel consistent and 5,000+ a day is where cold email becomes a MACHINE that books calls on autopilot
the math is brutally simple.
at a 0.1% booking rate, 1,000 emails gives you 1 call. 5,000 gives you 5\. 10,000 gives you 10
the booking rate stays roughly the same across every niche i've tested.
the only variable you actually control is how many emails you send so send more lmfao
you need infrastructure to support this though.
300-800 inboxes on full admin google workspace accounts. 60-80 domains. each inbox sending about 15 emails a day so no individual inbox gets burned.
the volume comes from having hundreds of inboxes running SIMULTANEOUSLY.
i personally run 665 inboxes sending 10k emails a day. setting this up takes about 10 minutes once you know what you're doing
##
3\. make the offer stupidly clear
vague offers die everythime
"we help businesses grow" is invisible in an inbox because it means NOTHING to anyone.
if a prospect can't understand what you're offering and why they should care in 5 seconds flat, you've lost them
the email template is four lines.
hey \[name\]. opener. irresistible offer. cta
that's the whole thing. the offer is the part that matters most. without something genuinely compelling the entire campaign ghosts.
make it hard to say no to.
"hey james, just checked and noticed you don't have a website, would you like one for free? want to show you what i got" books calls because saying yes costs the prospect absolutely nothing
just write like a real person with a real reason to reach out.
lowercase subject lines work better.
"hey {{firstname}}" and "something for {{firstname}}" CONSISTENTLY outperform anything that sounds like it came from a marketing department
##
4\. follow up like you have a screw loose
i run 3-5 follow ups MINIMUM on every campaign and each one reframes the offer slightly or adds a piece of value

Every developer building with the claude API has been through this.
You sit down to test something quick. Write the JSON body. Escape every string. Set the headers manually. Pipe it through jq just so you can read the output.
And that's just to send one message.
On June 2 2026, Anthropic released the ant CLI and made all of that optional.
One binary, written in Go, MIT licensed, open source.
Every Claude API endpoint accessible from your terminal. Messages, models, files, batch jobs, agents, sessions, environments, skills. All of it.
This is not a wrapper.
This is the operational layer for a platform that has been quietly shifting from model provider to full agent infrastructure since April.
Here is everything updated through June 2026 with every feature Anthropic has shipped since the original launch.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKNKIvHbgAAKvSB?format=png&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2063574218584018944/hey%5Fmadni/article/2063606029146034375/media/2063574568212856832)
##
What ant actually is
People keep comparing it to curl.
That comparison misses the point entirely.
curl gives you raw HTTP. You still have to build the request body, set every header, handle pagination yourself, and parse output with jq.
ant is a typed API client.
You pass flags → it builds the request → handles auth → paginates automatically → formats the response based on context.
Single binary, zero runtime dependencies. Drop it in your PATH and it works.
The code lives at
[github.com/anthropics/anthropic-cli](http://x.com/i/article/2063574218584018944//github.com/anthropics/anthropic-cli)
The command structure is consistent across everything {resource then action, colons for nested resources}:
```text
ant models list
ant messages create --model claude-opus-4-8 --max-tokens 1024
ant beta:agents retrieve --agent-id agent_01...
ant beta:sessions:events list --session-id session_01...
```
If you have used the GitHub CLI or the Stripe CLI, the pattern feels familiar within minutes.
Beta resources (agents, sessions, deployments, environments, skills, vaults, memory stores) all live under the beta: prefix.
The CLI automatically sends the correct anthropic-beta: managed-agents-2026-04-01 header for every beta command. You never touch the header yourself.
##
Installation
Under 5 minutes from zero to running.
![](https://pbs.twimg.com/tweet_video_thumb/HKNd2OcaIAAbgIx.jpg)
GIF
```text
macOS via Homebrew:
brew install anthropics/tap/ant
Linux or WSL:
curl -fsSL https://console.anthropic.com/install/cli | sh
Via Go:
go install github.com/anthropics/ant-cli@latest
Verify:
ant --version
```
![](https://pbs.twimg.com/tweet_video_thumb/HKNcebibkAAdlSz.jpg)
GIF
If you hit path errors on Linux or WSL, run these in order:
```text
# Check Go is installed
go version
# Find where the binary landed
ls $(go env GOPATH)/bin/ant
# Add to PATH
export PATH="$(go env GOPATH)/bin:$PATH"
# Make permanent
echo 'export PATH="$(go env GOPATH)/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc
```
One thing to know before you start; if ANTHROPIC\_API\_KEY is set as an environment variable and you also have a named pro

From Vibe Coding to Agentic Engineering: Building Production Systems with AI Agents
[![](https://pbs.twimg.com/profile_images/1907008174474825728/rYJaEnu__normal.jpg)](http://x.com/i/article/2063566081453694976/carlsue)

In February 2025, Andrej Karpathy described vibe coding as the practice of describing intent in natural language, accepting an LLM's changes with minimal review, and letting the code grow beyond your usual comprehension. It delivered impressive speed for personal projects and prototypes.
One year later he observed that agent capabilities had advanced, and proposed "agentic engineering" as his preferred name for the evolved practice of orchestrating agents while keeping strong human oversight of architecture and process. The goal, as he framed it, is to claim the leverage of agents without compromising software quality.
The distinction matters. Vibe coding works well for a single user on low-stakes personal work, but it quickly accumulates hidden debt, security gaps, and maintainability problems the moment other people depend on the result. Agentic engineering keeps the speed and leverage of modern agents, but anchors everything in clear structure, traceable artifacts, and human accountability.
##
The Agentic Engineering Workflow
Start with rough intent and carry on design conversations with the AI while documenting the functionality into design meeting notes describing the functionality into its component parts. Once the design feels solid, capture the high-level view and component map in a design hierarchy (this is what people are showing when they show an obsidian "brain") a navigable structure that gives both you and the agent ready access to surrounding context, related decisions, and dependencies. This is also where design diagrams live, such as UML (universal model language), code or user interaction flows, alongside links to architectural decision records (ADRs) where they clarify how components relate.
For each module or smallest functionality block, create a focused spec.md within the LLD that defines precise behavior, function signatures, edge cases, test expectations, and integration points. Using the whole structure as a design context prompt the AI to build a ticket style hierarchy with direct traceability back to the wiki pages and the specs. Implement ticket by ticket with the agent following the relevant spec.md as its contract. Then you run verification gates, deploy, observe, and update the living artifacts as requirements evolve.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKNFr-FXcAE-iEc?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2063566081453694976/carlsue/article/2063584716771541327/media/2063569675968016385)
##
Real Example: Daily Backup Verifier
Consider a small, production-grade CLI tool that verifies daily S3 backups and sends Slack alerts on failure.
Begin with the rough goal: "I need something reliable that checks my backups are healthy every day." Then carry on architectural conversations with the AI to surface requirements and edge cases:
* What are the realistic failure modes for S3 backups in practice?
* What exactly should we verify (age, file count, size, success rate), and what thresholds make sense?
* How should configuration and secrets be handled across local development and production IAM roles?
* What CLI commands and output formats would be useful day to day?

Most current AI agent frameworks operate primarily as applications built on top of large language models. They can perform reasoning, call tools, and maintain context within a session, but they generally lack robust, native mechanisms for long-term structured persistence, workload isolation, autonomous expansion of their own capabilities, and reliable coordination across multiple components over extended periods of time.
Hermes Agent, developed by Nous Research, implements several architectural features that set it apart from many other agent frameworks. These include support for persistent memory across sessions, the ability to run multiple isolated execution contexts through profiles, a structured task orchestration system based on Kanban, mechanisms that allow agents to create and store reusable procedures derived from their own activity, and a messaging gateway that connects the agent to 27+ communication platforms.
This article examines Hermes through the lens of a Personal AI Operating System. The goal is to provide a detailed and honest analysis of its core architectural layers, how these layers interact in practice, and what the system can realistically offer as of June 2026, based on publicly available documentation and observed behavior.
##
1\. Core Layers of Hermes
To better understand the structure of Hermes, it is helpful to map its components to concepts from traditional operating systems.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKOCpBNWMAATjfB?format=jpg&name=900x900)](http://x.com/i/article/2063630561466265600/IBuzovskyi/article/2063645563241844823/media/2063636695476482048)
##
1.1 Memory Architecture
Hermes maintains multiple distinct memory layers instead of attempting to keep all relevant information inside a single context window. The main types include:
* Session Memory: Context that is active during a specific task or conversation. This type of memory is typically short-lived and tied to the current session.
* Long-term Memory: Persistent storage of facts, insights, user preferences, and accumulated knowledge that survives across sessions and system restarts. Capped by configurable limits to prevent unbounded growth:
yaml
```yaml
memory:
memory_enabled: true
user_profile_enabled: true
memory_char_limit: 2200 # ~800 tokens
user_char_limit: 1375 # ~500 tokens
```
* Skill Memory: Storage of structured, reusable procedures (skills) that the agent has created or refined based on past successful work. Stored as plain markdown files in \~/.hermes/skills/.
* Session Recall: FTS5 full-text search with LLM summarization across the entire conversation history. Query any past session:
> Remind me of every business idea we discussed last month. What was the competitor analysis we ran 3 weeks ago?
The multi-layered memory approach is one of the foundational elements that allows Hermes to function more like a persistent system than a typical conversational agent.
External Memory Providers:
For use cases that require deeper intelligence beyond built-in memory, Hermes supports 8 external memory provider plugins:
* Mem0 — knowledge graph + semantic retrieval. Loads only relevant entries per

Remotion was the first tool that let me ship a real launch video from a terminal, and I fell hard. Every video I made this spring started as a React composition. Then HyperFrames came along, and somewhere around the Granola CLI demo and the Agent Cookie launch reel, it quietly took over my whole video workflow. I felt a little guilty about it. So I did what I always do before I trust a feeling: I ran
[/last30days](https://github.com/mvanhorn/last30days-skill)
on Remotion prompting, on HyperFrames, and on the head-to-head, and read what the community actually says.
The verdict surprised me: the community is not having the fight I expected. Both tools are winning, for different jobs, and the people getting the best results out of each one follow prompting playbooks that have quietly converged into doctrine. This article is the verdict, the receipts, and both playbooks.
##
🥊 The verdict the community already reached: stop picking sides
The sharpest framing in the whole corpus came from Markandey Sharma:
> HyperFrames vs Remotion isn't about tools it's about the medium. HyperFrames uses HTML, which LLMs naturally understand. (Markandey Sharma, May 2026)
That is the entire debate in two sentences. Remotion (49K stars, shipping since 2021) bets that video should be typed React components, written by developers, reviewed like code, rendered at hyperscale on Lambda. HyperFrames (25K stars in roughly two months since HeyGen open sourced it) bets that the author is no longer a developer. The author is an agent, and agents grew up on HTML. HeyGen engineer Joshua Xu's rationale, per Nidhin's deep dive: LLMs are trained on oceans of HTML, while React plus Remotion is a sliver of the training data.
And the community has stopped treating that as a war. Sabrina Ramonov lists them as items 1 and 2 of the same "unlimited free AI videos" stack (19K views on TikTok this week alone). Hermes ships both as built-in video skills: Remotion for programmatic motion graphics, HyperFrames for quick compositions. Corey Haines built a router skill that picks between HeyGen, Remotion, HyperFrames, and Runway per request. Even HyperFrames' own comparison guide credits Remotion for pioneering the rendering patterns it builds on: headless Chrome, frame-by-frame capture, FFmpeg encoding.
Nobody serious is asking which one wins. They are asking which one fits the job in front of them. The honest answer to both questions lives in what each community says about its own tool.
##
🎬 What /last30days pulled up on Remotion
The Remotion story this month is a mature project having its creator moment. Jonny Burger announced the milestone himself:
> Remotion has passed the break-even point! We've recouped our investments and are now in the green. (
>
> [@JNYBGR](https://x.com/@JNYBGR)
>
> , May 26, 2026)
Five years of work, now sustainable, and shipping: the new version has visual editing with two-way sync between code and preview, where code is always the source of truth. The agent skill, remotion-dev/skills, turned a React framework into a creator phenomenon. Sabrina's Remotion reel did 152K views on TikTok plus 61K

A full breakdown of how one open-source tool cuts your Claude Code session costs by 2.5x, without any changes to CLAUDE(.)md, prompts, or models (covered with a setup guide and why it is effective).
MCPMark V2 surfaced something counterintuitive.
Moving Claude from Sonnet 4.5 to Sonnet 4.6, the smarter model, pushed backend token usage through Supabase’s MCP server from 11.6M to 17.9M across the same 21 database tasks.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKMdDc0aQAANOAP?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2061735436687736832/%5Favichawla/article/2063548691353629040/media/2063524999378649088)
The model got smarter, but the backend token usage actually increased.
The reason is subtle, and it has nothing to do with the model.
Instead, it has to do with how the backend exposes info to the agent. When context is incomplete, a more capable model doesn’t just skip the gap.
Instead, it reasons harder about it, runs more discovery queries, and retries more often. So missing context gets more expensive as models improve, not less.
Let’s look at why a traditional backend makes the agent work harder, what backend context engineering should look like, and what the cost difference is on a real project.
#
Why Firebase makes the agent work harder
Firebase is a solid backend.
But it wasn’t built to be operated by a coding agent, and three of its assumptions turn into token costs when an agent takes over the workflow.
##
1) The tool surface and its docs inflate the context
The usual way to give a coding agent Firebase access is the official Firebase MCP server, built into firebase-tools. It ships more than 50 tools and activates the ones for your project automatically.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKMdHGjbMAEJfBW?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2061735436687736832/%5Favichawla/article/2063548691353629040/media/2063525062121304065)
Connecting it loads that tool manifest into the agent’s context before any work starts, and the server also exposes documentation resources that get pulled into the session on its own.
The manifest grows with Firebase's product surface, not with whatever you happen to be building, so even a small app that touches one or two services still carries definitions for Crashlytics, Remote Config, App Hosting, and the rest.
##
2) No single view of backend state
Firebase has no “show me the whole backend” call.
Instead, the state is spread across separate commands like
* firebase projects:list
* apps:list
* apps:sdkconfig
* firestore:databases:get
* firestore:indexes, and more.
Firestore makes this worse by being schemaless.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKMjntra4AARyKc?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2061735436687736832/%5Favichawla/article/2063548691353629040/media/2063532219449401344)
There’s no declared shape to read, so an agent infers a collection’s fields and types from sample documents rather than querying a schema.
It stitches info together from many partial calls, and that fragmented discovery pattern compounds, since each call returns only a slice, and some of it need

Tweet: https://x.com/Blum_OG/status/2063313653504565361 Image URLs: - https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2063313558620794880/img/6SWP1_TQJakq2fQl.jpg Linked content: - https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2063313558620794880/img/6SWP1_TQJakq2fQl.jpg: https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2063313558620794880/img/6SWP1_TQJakq2fQl.jpg
item.content:encoded:
Blum (@Blum_OG)

the hard part of multi-agent systems isn't building agents

it's knowing which agent in a 20-step chain actually helped

if you only get a result at the very end

there's no obvious way to trace back who deserved credit

EOM from Harvard solves this with one rule:
> when agent B takes over from agent A, B pays A from its wallet
> if B's move sets things up so that agent C is willing to pay a lot - B profits too

agents get rewarded for setting up good next steps

not just for finishing the task themselves

the result on accelerator design:
> the system discovered a useful design pattern on its own
> no template, no instructions - just payment rules and trial and error

the lesson:
> if your pipeline only produces a result at the end of a long chain,
> the bottleneck is usually "who gets credit for what", not the prompts

a market-based training loop can figure out the right agent sequence

that you'd otherwise have to design by hand

Privacy isn’t a prompt — it’s enforced by code. The Containment Guard physically blocks sensitive data from leaving its designated zones.

Codex did not become interesting only because the model got stronger.
It became interesting because the product layer started feeling calmer.
As of June 6, 2026, the clean update is this:
• Codex is now centered around GPT-5.5
• OpenAI recommends GPT-5.5 for complex Codex work
• Codex has app, CLI, IDE, cloud, Windows, browser, computer-use, plugins, sites, and annotations
• Claude Code has moved past the Opus 4.7 moment and now has Opus 4.8
• Opus 4.8 adds dynamic workflows, effort control, and better behavior on agentic tasks
This should not be read as:
"Codex won and Claude lost."
The better read:
Codex is winning trust in repo-heavy work because the harness is easier to reason about.
Claude Code still has serious power, but the user has to think harder about model choice, effort level, rate limits, tool permissions, and update channels.
That is the real story.
For coding agents, trust is now part of intelligence.
#
The model frame changed
Opus 4.7 was at the center of the argument in May 2026.
It is no longer the current model frame.
Anthropic released Claude Opus 4.8 on May 28, 2026.
That changes the comparison.
Opus 4.8 is not just a benchmark refresh. Anthropic says it improves on Opus 4.7, keeps regular pricing unchanged, adds effort control, launches dynamic workflows for Claude Code, and makes fast mode cheaper than previous models.
That matters because the trust problem was clear:
users felt Claude Code became unpredictable
The current Anthropic answer is:
give users more control over effort, let Claude Code run larger dynamic workflows, and ship a stronger Opus model
That does not erase the trust problem.
It updates it.
The question is no longer whether Opus 4.7 was the villain.
The question is whether Claude Code can make the right usage pattern obvious enough that users do not have to reverse-engineer the product.
#
The current Codex frame
OpenAI's Codex docs now list GPT-5.5 as the recommended starting model for complex coding, computer use, knowledge work, and research workflows.
That is the key update.
Codex is not just a GPT-5.3 Codex story anymore.
The current model stack is:
• \`gpt-5.5\` for complex Codex work
• \`gpt-5.4\` for strong professional work
• \`gpt-5.4-mini\` for faster lower-cost coding tasks
• \`gpt-5.3-codex-spark\` as a near-instant research preview for Pro users
OpenAI also says older \`gpt-5.2\` and \`gpt-5.3-codex\` references are deprecated in Codex sign-in workflows.
That means older comparisons need to be handled carefully.
If a test used an old Codex model, it is not describing the product today.
The current Codex advantage is not just raw model strength.
It is the product shape:
• worktrees
• reviewable diffs
• app, CLI, IDE, and cloud surfaces
• \`AGENTS.md\` project instructions
• in-app browser
• computer use
• plugins and skills
• remote connections
• sites and annotations for workspace output
That is why Codex feels more like an engineering system than a chat assistant.
It gives the model a place to operate.
#
AGENTS.md is the trust layer
The mechanism is harness engineering.

Industry research usually lives across annual reports, earnings calls, market studies, spreadsheets, and browser tabs.
Well, the information exists. The connections disappear.
NotebookLM can turn that document pile into one focused research system. You choose the evidence, define the analyst's job, and ask the same questions every quarter.
Standard NotebookLM accounts support 50 sources per notebook. Deep Research also runs inside NotebookLM, so it can search the web, prepare a report, and suggest sources for the notebook.
A useful first version needs around 15 documents.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKSYGIAWUAADP_F?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2063916662223470592/xanaxmontanaonx/article/2063949009899659761/media/2063941760238112768)
#
Build the source base
So, start with three layers.
Layer 1: companies
Add annual reports from 5-7 listed companies across the value chain. Include a large operator, a regional player, a supplier, and a specialist business.
This gives the notebook different business models instead of seven versions of the same company.
Layer 2: industry structure
Create three Deep Research reports before you start asking company-level questions. In practice, these reports become the background knowledge for everything that follows.
The first one is the history report:
```text
ROLE
You are an economic historian and industry analyst.
TASK
Write a factual, data-based history of [INDUSTRY].
Explain how the industry formed, why it matters economically, which forces shaped it, how major winners appeared, and which cycles repeat over time.
Cover:
• formation and early need
• first technologies, financing models, and institutions
• scale breakthroughs and standardization
• crises, regulation, consolidation, and profitability
• leading firms, market share changes, mergers, and breakups
• digital transformation and new entrants
• regional differences, trade, subsidies, and geography
• capital intensity, debt use, returns, and valuation patterns
• lessons for long-term investors
Use clear cause-and-effect analysis. Support claims with numbers and citations.
```
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKSU8xDXYAAzeLq?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2063916662223470592/xanaxmontanaonx/article/2063949009899659761/media/2063938300923043840)
The second one is the future report:
```text
Act as an industry strategist.
Analyze [INDUSTRY] today and the next 5-10 years.
Cover demand growth, supply limits, pricing power, regulation, technology shifts, automation, new entrants, customer behavior, margin pressure, capex needs, and possible disruption.
Give 3 scenarios:
• base case
• upside case

item.content:encoded:
Viv (@Vtrivedy10)

imo there’s a pretty solid default recipe that everyone should use to optimize a system of
Agent = Model + Harness

you should “train” both

1. Build v1 agent using a sensible base harness and some task specific prompting + tools

2. Harness Engineering using eval tasks that roughly match prod

this is often enough - most companies can get acceptable perf doing this. then they collect traces, mine them for patterns, and make slight tweaks from there

3. SFT using data collected from traces) or synthetic data. Often is good candidate for “distillation tasks” to train a cheaper model while maintaining existing performance

4. RL if you have the bandwidth and ability and desire to create environments and designing rewards that represents the tasks you want your agent to be good at. Push past the SFT behavior of “copying” data from existing model to pushing past in some dimension

5. Light harness engineering again to squeeze any more juice (ex: slight prompting) using the trained model that’s better at your task distribution

this loop will largely be productized as a general purpose recipe for building and improving agents

we’re still in the earliest innings of the world’s companies getting comfortable with steps 1-2 of this loop. Harness engineering will probably be the dominant way ppl will optimize agents

but i expect a large number of companies to onboard through this entire loop on some trial project of interest in the next year

most mfs will grind their DMs, send hundreds of messages a week, and post the occasional random thing on their profile because someone told them they "should be posting."
so their content does nothing.
it's a few disconnected posts with no strategy, consistency, or real purpose, sitting on a profile that prospects glance at and forget.
and then they conclude content doesn't work lol.
now, they're half right.
lazy content genuinely does nothing.
but content done properly is one of the most powerful revenue tools you have, and it does 3 things outbound alone can't.
it books calls on its own, pulling in warm inbound from people who found you rather than the other way around.
it makes your outbound convert better, because every prospect you message checks your profile, and strong content is what convinces them you're worth replying to.
it compounds, building an audience and a reputation over time so that your pipeline keeps getting easier instead of resetting to zero every month.
so let me break down how to make content actually print:
##
Why Content And Outbound Work Better Together
before the how, you need to understand why content matters even if outbound is your main engine.
every single prospect you reach out to does one thing before they reply. they click your profile to see who you are.
what they find in that moment decides whether the conversation goes anywhere.
if they land on a profile with nothing on it, no posts, no proof you know your space, just a name and a job title, your message loses credibility instantly. you look like every other random person sliding into their DMs.
if they land on a profile with a steady stream of sharp, relevant content that proves you deeply understand the problem you solve, your message gains credibility. now you're not a stranger pitching them, you're someone who clearly knows their world, reaching out.
so even if you never wanted content to be a lead source on its own, it still raises your reply rate on everything else you do. it's the credibility layer underneath your entire outbound effort.
and that's before content starts booking calls on its own, which it will once it's running properly.
##
The 3 Types Of Content That Actually Book Calls
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKKasPsXYAAP4Zj?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2063369932725796864/freddiexpott/article/2063386291606012208/media/2063381664206643200)
here's where most people go wrong. they post randomly, no structure, no plan, just whatever comes to mind that day.
content that prints is built around 3 specific types, each with a job. you want a mix of all 3, because together they move a stranger from never having heard of you to trusting you enough to have a conversation.
1\. Personal Posts
these are about your journey, your story, your unique takes on your industry.
their job is to build connection. people buy from people, and if you only ever post pure information, you become a faceless account nobody feels anything about. personal posts make prospects feel like they know you, which is what makes them comfortable reaching out.
this isn't about overs

item.content:encoded:
Vox (@Voxyz_ai)

tools go stale. here's how they evolve instead.

workflows change. models change. your standards change. rules you write today might be wrong in three weeks. so every tool needs a patch loop.

didn't trigger when it should have → fix the trigger
triggered when it shouldn't → narrow the scope
used outdated info → update the source of truth
same mistake keeps happening → add a failure mode
you keep editing the same thing by hand → turn that edit into a rule
hasn't been used in a while → archive it

the return on tooling comes from compounding. compounding comes from updating.

This blog is probably going to offend some people.
Good.
Because honestly, I am tired of watching the same cycle repeat every year.
Students enter college with big dreams.
Four years later, most of them leave with excuses.
And before someone starts typing "bro you are generalizing," yes, obviously not everyone.
But if you are from an engineering background, especially a tier-3 or tier-69 college, you know exactly what I am talking about.
This is not a motivational blog.
This is not a "follow your passion" blog.
This is just a collection of observations from my own journey, my friends, people I have worked with, and thousands of students I have seen online.
So let's talk.
For better reading experience read it here:
[Dear Indian Students](https://ramx.in/blog/dear-indian-students)
##
The Dead Crowd
Walk into most engineering classrooms.
Half the class is sleeping.
The other half is scrolling Instagram.
Nobody gives a shit about what is being taught.
And to be fair, most professors don't seem very excited either.
Everybody is just trying to get through the day.
But the problem goes deeper than bad professors.
The real issue is that our education system trained us to memorize, not to explore.
School rewarded us for remembering things.
Not questioning things.
Not building things.
Not experimenting.
Just remember the answer.
Write the answer.
Get the marks.
Repeat.
JEE, boards, entrance exams everything optimized us for scores, not curiosity. So when people enter college, they are already mentally exhausted.
They're waiting for instructions.
* Which course should I watch?
* Which language should I learn?
* Which project should I build?
* Which company should I target?
Every decision is outsourced.
If you want my detailed answers to most of these questions, I wrote an entire FAQ Blog:
[The FAQ](https://ramx.in/blog/faq)
Very few people actually sit down and think:
"What do I want to learn?"
I realized this pretty early.
Within the first few months of college, I figured out something that changed everything for me.
This college is probably not going to get me where I want to go.
And after talking to people from other colleges, I realized something even funnier.
Most colleges are playing the same game.
Different building.
Different logo.
Same shit.
The only thing I could control was myself.
So in the middle of my first year, I started grinding.
Not web development. Not AI. Not any of the trendy stuff.
Graphic design and video editing.
My goal was simple.
Earn money.
Because I knew one thing.
If I wanted freedom to experiment, take risks, build weird things, fail, learn and try again, I needed financial independence.
Nobody was going to hand it to me.
That mindset got me my first internship.
Not because I was special. Not because I was smarter.
I simply accepted reality earlier than most people.
If you want the full story, read my blog:
[How to be me?](https://ramx.in/blog/how-to-be-me-learn-build-and-crush-it)
The biggest lesson?
Nobody is coming to save you.
Not your college. Not your professors. Not your friends.
Certainly not some random YouTube playlist.
##
The Crab Mentality Problem
The second

the people who say it's dead are sending 50 emails a day from 3 inboxes wondering why nobody replies lol

real cold email is 500+ inboxes sending 10,000 emails a day with a simple offer that makes it hard to say no.
the math works every single time IF you give it enough volume to work with
##
why volume beats everything:

how many calls do you want per month?
if you want 10 calls a month, you need to send about 10,000 emails per month.

if you want 300 calls a month, you need 200,000+ emails per month. 6,500+ a day. 500+ inboxes.
this is where we operate (my agency)
at this volume it's GENUINELY hard to fail because the math won't let you
cold email is not broken lmfaoo. 200 emails a day is broken.

skills tend to be discussed interchangeably with CLI tools or MCP servers. That's not incorrect. Skills are, in fact, complementary to those approaches
##
1\. It's just a bunch of .md files
Yes, which makes it ultra-distributable (inside your repo, as part of your NPM package or
[skill.sh](http://x.com/i/article/2063273395320750080//skill.sh)
). You can version-control them if you want and you can also ship them with your MCP server / CLI tools
Skills aren't limited to just .md files. The
[skills spec](https://agentskills.io/)
allows you to add literally any file as part of the skill. So your skills can ship images, assets, scripts, apps and literally anything as part of your skill
##
2\. Progressive disclosure
This is the cool bit. The skill implicitly has a 3-tiered approach to being used.
* First, when the skill isn't loaded, the model only sees the "name" and the "description" of the skill. This lets the agent choose when to activate the skill
* Then, when it does activate (and depending on your harness's implementation), it only loads the SKILL.md file's content + the structure of the skill.
* The agent can then decide which files it wants to read into its context and / or stuff it wants to execute. Selective retrieval.
This is super powerful because context windows stay lean and relevant.
##
3\. Skills encode Operating Policy
Why can't I just ship a --help command to my CLI tool? This is a great argument and something I see all the time. The difference here is that skills aren't just meant to be "documentation" (I mean you can treat them as docs but that's up to you)
A help command will typically list out the tool's capabilities, but it won't tell the agent what the best / intended way to use it is. You can ship skills with your CLI tools meant to be used by agents that describe possible workflows and capabilities
##
4\. They're multi-purpose
You can model a lot of use-cases just out of skills
It could be a prompt template / simple task: this is how I use skills 90% of the time. It's often an adjective like "create-draft-pr" that tell the agent to create a PR my way
Or it could be documentation, benefitting from the progressive disclosure point. Or it could also model entire workflows: incident response, release procedures, and research processes since you can ship executables or reference tools as part of the skill
So implementing a single spec in your harness unlocks a whole bunch of workflows that are also largely portable across harnesses
##
Downsides
It's not all roses. Much like CLI tools, the downside to skills is that it needs access to something resembling a file-system, and depending on what your skill ships, it might also need the ability to execute commands. Also, Skills themselves do not execute anything.
MCP on the other hand gets around this problem by just requiring a transport-protocol which exposes and calls tools (MCP also has other trade-offs but those are out of scope for this article)

##
Stop trying to reinvent electricity.
If you're anything like me, you've spent way too much time hunting for the "perfect" business idea. The unicorn. The blue ocean nobody has touched or even thought of yet.
And if you're really anything like me, you've also quietly judged the people making money off ideas that look almost embarrassingly simple from the outside (the Notion templates, the cold email agencies, the niche newsletters) while you were busy trying to invent something nobody had ever seen before.
I'm not here to talk down on you. I did this for years. I had notebooks full of ideas that were supposed to be "the one." I had a graveyard of half-built products that nobody asked for, all because I was convinced that the only path to a meaningful income was to stumble onto something nobody had ever stumbled onto before.
The unfortunate reality is that this belief is the single biggest thing that keeps people broke.
Because while you're trying to invent electricity for the second time, the person two steps ahead of you is just plugging things into the wall.
This essay is something I actually want you to sit with, because it changed the entire trajectory of my life when it finally clicked.
Let's begin.
##
If it is humanly possible, it is possible for you
> "We become what we behold. We shape our tools, and thereafter our tools shape us". – Marshall McLuhan
About four years ago I was scrolling Twitter and stumbled on this guy with a faceless profile picture casually tweeting that he'd made $9,000 that month from selling Notion templates.
At the time I had no idea what that even was. I clicked his profile out of pure curiosity, and that single click ended up being the day my entire life changed.
Because here was this random guy, no different from me in any meaningful way, just sharing his journey, occasionally dropping products, and printing money in the process.
The truth is that I've always operated from one core belief that has shaped just about every decision I've made since I was a teenager:
If it is humanly possible, it is possible for me too.
Anything a human can do, I can do.
This sounds like a Pinterest quote, but I want you to actually sit with it for a second, because most people read this kind of line and nod along without ever internalizing what it actually means.
Let's run through an example.
Take Usain Bolt. For 15 years he has been the only human being to run 100m in 9.58 seconds. By any conventional logic, the belief I should hold is that I will never beat that record. He's the fastest. End of conversation.
But hear me out on this one (call me a disillusioned egomaniac if you want), if I truly decided I wanted to beat his record, I genuinely believe I could.
And yes, I'm 28 next year and I'd be the first to admit my window for sprinting is probably already closed. But in theory? If I put in double the training he did over the years, why couldn't I? If I dedicated my entire existence to it. If I structured every meal, every recovery session, every micro-decision around that one outcome, the math says it's possible.
That's the belief I have.
"Another human did this, there

🔗 Designing, Refining, and Maintaining Agent Skills at Perplexity

research
Designing, Refining, and Maintaining Agent Skills at Perplexity
Perplexity’s frontier agent products rest on a foundation of know-how and domain expertise packaged in modular [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io/home). We maintain a carefully curated library of Skills across our technical environments. These Skills include many of the general-purpose utilities powering [Perplexity Computer](https://www.perplexity.ai/products/computer); vertical-specific capabilities in areas such as finance, law, and health; and a very long tail of modules for addressing user needs. Some Skills are infrequently invoked but critical when invoked. To ensure a consistently excellent user experience, Perplexity’s Agents team prioritizes Skill quality just as much as code quality.
The intuitions and best practices required to develop a high-quality Skill differ significantly from those required to build traditional software. The Agents team reviews many pull requests from excellent engineers who develop Skills in the course of their work. The result is almost always numerous comments and suggestions for revision. This is because many useful patterns for writing code become antipatterns in Skill creation.
For example, if you take some of the aphorisms from [PEP20 – The Zen of Python](https://peps.python.org/pep-0020/), it quickly becomes clear that writing good Python code is unlike writing good Skills. Of the 20 lines of wisdom, at least half are fully wrong or actively misleading when writing Skills. Here are five of them:
Zen of Python | Zen of Skills |
|---|---|
Simple is better than complex | A Skill is a folder, not a file. Complexity is the feature. |
Explicit is better than implicit | Activation is implicit pattern matching. Progressive disclosure. |
Sparse is better than dense | Context is expensive. Maximum signal per token. |
Special cases aren’t special enough to break the rules | Gotchas ARE the special cases (they're the highest-value content). |
If the implementation is easy to explain, it may be a good idea | If it's easy to explain, the model already knows it. Delete it. |
This guide is the document that engineers across Perplexity use when developing and reviewing Skills. We’re also releasing this guide to the public so that our discoveries and learnings can benefit the broader community. Whether you’re an engineer designing production Skills in your day-to-day work, a Computer user looking to develop your own Skill in an area you know best, or both, this guide is for you.
What is a Skill?
When you write a Skill, you aren’t writing plain old software (even though Skills are now part of the main logical engines for agent systems). Rather, you're building context for models and their environments. A Skill has different constraints and different design principles. If you write a Skill like you do code, you will fail.
A Skill is at least four things, especially in the context of how we build them at Perplexity.
A Skill is a Directory
A Skill is not just a single SKILL.md
file. In many cases, a Skill includes several files. Under the directory named after your Skill, you might have:
SKILL.md
: frontmatter and instructionsscripts/
: code the agent runs, not reinventsreferences/
: heavy docs, loaded conditionallyassets/
: templates, schemas, and dataconfig.json
: first-run user setup
This hub-and-spoke pattern allows you to keep Skills very focused and tight, and one can use the folder structure in a very creative way. Sometimes, particularly intricate Skills benefit from multiple levels of hierarchy to help the model navigate better. Suppose a Skill requires knowledge across 300 topics, groupable into 20 subject matter areas. Reliably choosing the right topic among 300 is an unsolved challenge even for today’s best frontier models. It’s a much easier choice problem for a model to hone in on one of 20 areas, than among the 15 topics within that area.
As one example of how multilevel hierarchy provides value, our team employed th

Tweet: https://x.com/ericosiu/status/2063316993101480353 Image URLs: - https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2063103304247205888/img/t_5qt255teOLMClU.jpg Linked content: - https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2063103304247205888/img/t_5qt255teOLMClU.jpg: https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2063103304247205888/img/t_5qt255teOLMClU.jpg - Leveling Up: https://newsletter.levelingup.com/
item.content:encoded:
ericosiu (@ericosiu)

I spent 30 minutes a day with one person on my team. Did that 10 to 15 times.

That person started doing the work of four or five people.

No micromanagement. No constant check-ins. They just executed without me pushing.

So I asked myself: why am I not doing this at scale?

That question led me to build what I'm calling the "Pod of One apprenticeship" at Single Grain.

I pick a small group of the most talented, AI-forward operators on my team. I spend real one-on-one time with them. I share my speed, my expectations, my frameworks. Then they go train the next layer of the org.

Jedi training, basically. You teach the ones who can teach.

I asked one of the people I trained how impactful it was. He said 9/10. I didn't think much of the time I was putting in. He thought it was massive.

That gap in perception is the whole point. Founders often underestimate how much signal they carry just by being in the room.

I rolled this out this week and it's already one of the higher leverage things I've done.

🔗 Leveling Up

##

[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKI1bgBXoAE6kCN?format=jpg&name=900x900)](http://x.com/i/article/2063265407838957569/Voxyz%5Fai/article/2063289940310372596/media/2063270325857525761)
Turn the stuff you keep asking Claude Code/Codex to do into actual tools
[![](https://pbs.twimg.com/profile_images/1998303259279138816/5bqsxKJS_normal.jpg)](http://x.com/i/article/2063265407838957569/Voxyz%5Fai)
[Vox](http://x.com/i/article/2063265407838957569/Voxyz%5Fai)
[@Voxyz\_ai](http://x.com/i/article/2063265407838957569/Voxyz%5Fai)
·
13h
Follow
Click to Follow Voxyz\_ai
4
7
65
[8.2K](http://x.com/i/article/2063265407838957569/Voxyz%5Fai/status/2063289940310372596/analytics)
You probably asked AI to do a few of these last week:
Turn a bug report into an assignable ticket. Review a chunk of code. Merge info from three different places into one summary. Check something before you send it out. Prioritize a pile of customer messages. Pull numbers from a few data sources and see what moved.
First time, totally normal.
Second time, still fine.
By the third time you're copy-pasting the same prompt, that task has a pattern.
A pattern means you can leave a tool behind.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKI1fbaWsAAro9i?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2063265407838957569/Voxyz%5Fai/article/2063289940310372596/media/2063270393339621376)
The tool doesn't have to be big. It could be a test runner script, a deploy-preflight.md, a triage-checklist.md, a
[SKILL.md](https://developers.openai.com/codex/skills)
, a new rule in your AGENTS.md, or a metrics checklist that runs once a day.
The point is that next time the same kind of work comes up, Claude Code/Codex doesn't have to guess your standards.
It should read directly from your project:
How this task starts. What the inputs are. What good output looks like. Which file is the source of truth. What it can do automatically. Where it must stop and wait for a human.
##
One-off conversations don't compound
A lot of people use Claude Code/Codex as a fancy chat window.
Today:
> Turn this bug report into an assignable ticket.
Tomorrow:
> Compare these three options and tell me which one has the least risk.
Day after:
> Pull this week's numbers and flag anything that dropped.
Each time it saves you a little time.
But each time you have to re-explain the standards.
Tickets need repro steps and a priority level. Comparisons need clear tradeoffs laid out. Metrics need to be compared against last week, not just raw numbers. Passing locally doesn't mean it's safe to ship. Anything public-facing needs to stop before human approval.
That's the cost of repeating yourself.
A better approach: after each task, leave something in the project folder that makes the next time easier.
Triage a bug today, leave behind a triage checklist. Compare options today, leave behind a decision template. Pull metrics today, leave behind a weekly metrics script. Catch AI overstepping a boundary today, write that approval gate into AGENTS.md.
After every task, the project should know a little more.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKI1iDqWAAA38bH?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2063265407838957569/Voxyz%5Fai/article/2063289940310372596/media/2063270438503841792)
##
Define the result first, then the steps
I wouldn't start by writing:
plaintext
```plaintext
1. Gather info
2. Make a decision
3. Output the result
```
That's too vague. AI reads that and still has to guess what you actually want.
A better starting point is to describe what "done" looks like.
Say you want it to prioritize bugs. Don't just say "tell me which bugs are important."
Write it like this:
plaintext
```plaintext
Goal:
Determine the priority of this bug report.
Inputs:
- Bug description and repro steps
- Blast radius (how many users

At their best these communities are not just negative: childfree spaces can be about autonomy, choice and acceptance, anti-car spaces about safer streets and transit, and LLM-skeptical developer spaces about the future of labor, code quality and...
item.content:encoded:
Armin Ronacher ⇌ (@mitsuhiko)

Some weekend thoughts of recent mob behaviors. https://lucumr.pocoo.org/2026/6/6/communities-of-not/

🔗 Communities of Not | Armin Ronacher's Thoughts and Writings

Armin Ronacher 's Thoughts and Writings blog archive projects travel talks about Communities of Not written on June 06, 2026 There is a strange thing that happens in communities that gather around abstinence from something: identity from opposition. At their best these communities are not just negative: childfree spaces can be about autonomy, choice and acceptance, anti-car spaces about safer streets and transit, and LLM-skeptical developer spaces about the future of labor, code quality and slop 1 . But the thing being refused often does not go away and instead becomes the main subject of the community’s identity. That would be fine if it stayed at criticism, maybe even angry criticism, but more often than not it turns into policing and hatred towards others. An influencer without children becomes a parent, an urban bike commuter by choice buys a Porsche, a respected developer tries LLMs, and the community feels betrayed because it assumed they were members of the same tribe. The expulsion of that person (who never signed up to be a community member) is entirely imaginary but the punishment that the community unleashes is not: people pile on and shame them, quote them out of context and turn their weakest moments into proof that the person was always unserious, a sharlatan or should not be listened to. I do not think the answer is to tell people to stop paying attention. Cars shape cities even for people who cycle, children influence politics, workplaces and taxes even for people who do not have them. For us developers, LLMs show up in editors, issue trackers, hiring conversations, management pressure and code reviews whether we asked for them or not. Resisting that can be legitimate but that is no excuse for using one’s rejection to justify shitty mob behavior. I understand the thinking all too well, because I have done versions of this myself in the past. It took me a while to become more accepting of other people’s worldviews that diverge from mine. Whatever insecurities we have, finding a group of others sharing them can be comforting. The danger is that being part of a crowd of negativity can easily make us part of collective harassment. I can only encourage you to breathe, slow down, de-escalate when given the chance, and resist the temptation to always assume the most catastrophic reading. Default to being open to new things . Being negative towards something, and making that ones identity, is an easy trap to fall into. These examples are not meant as equivalents. The recent mob against rsync is the LLM version that prompted this post. I picked the others because I’m familiar with those communities and they all show similar cases of personal choices being interpreted as betrayal. ↩ This entry was tagged ai and thoughts copy as / view markdown © Copyright 2026 by Armin Ronacher. item.content:encoded:
Daniel San (@dani_avila7)

http://x.com/i/article/2063325372775575552

🔗 http://x.com/i/article/2063325372775575552

##
To view keyboard shortcuts, press question mark
[View keyboard shortcuts](http://x.com/i/article/2063325372775575552/i/keyboard%5Fshortcuts)
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKJsyqUXYAEvrIY?format=jpg&name=900x900)](http://x.com/i/article/2063325372775575552/dani%5Favila7/article/2063336153630011728/media/2063331196898074625)
How NVIDIA's SkillSpector works and How to add It to your skill PRs
[![](https://pbs.twimg.com/profile_images/1952921529504649216/RYHFCSSM_normal.jpg)](http://x.com/i/article/2063325372775575552/dani%5Favila7)
[Daniel San](http://x.com/i/article/2063325372775575552/dani%5Favila7)
[@dani\_avila7](http://x.com/i/article/2063325372775575552/dani%5Favila7)
·
9h
·
Follow
Click to Follow dani\_avila7
2
10
84
[10K](http://x.com/i/article/2063325372775575552/dani%5Favila7/status/2063336153630011728/analytics)
AI agents run code they didn't write. Skills, tools, MCP servers, prompts pulled from external repos. The attack surface is real, and most teams aren't thinking about it yet.
NVIDIA's SkillSpector is their answer, and this is how you run it.
##
What it is
SkillSpector is a static security scanner built for AI agent skills (Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, Cursor, and similar). It answers one question: is this skill safe to install?
Repo:
<https://github.com/nvidia/skillspector>
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKJtZyPWYAA3KW-?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2063325372775575552/dani%5Favila7/article/2063336153630011728/media/2063331869039419392)
It analyzes the SKILL.md and every script in the folder, runs 64 detection patterns across 16 categories, and produces a risk score from 0 to 100 with a clear verdict. Apache-2.0, so you can read exactly what it's doing.
##
How it works
The scanner builds a context from the skill folder, then runs analyzers in parallel:
* Prompt injection and instruction overrides
* Data exfiltration (env var harvesting, context leakage, external transmission)
* Supply chain (curl | bash, CVEs via
[OSV.dev](http://x.com/i/article/2063325372775575552//OSV.dev)
, typosquatting)
* Behavioral AST (eval, exec, subprocess, dynamic imports)
* Taint tracking (credentials flowing to the network, file read to exfiltration)
* YARA signatures for malware, webshells, cryptominers
* MCP-specific patterns: tool poisoning, unicode deception, least-privilege violations
Scoring is additive: LOW +5, MEDIUM +10, HIGH +25, CRITICAL +50\. A single CRITICAL pattern puts you at 50 before anything else is counted.
If executable scripts are present, the total is multiplied by 1.3\. The final number maps to a verdict on a 0–100 scale, anything above 50 is blocked automatically.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKJt7DmWYAAR0HB?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2063325372775575552/dani%5Favila7/article/2063336153630011728/media/2063332440634974208)
Reports come out as terminal output, JSON, Markdown, or SARIF, which is what makes it drop into CI cleanly.
##
Adding it to your Skill PRs
SkillSpector plugs into GitHub Actions without much ceremony.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKJwbnlWgAAVRf_?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2063325372775575552/dani%5Favila7/article/2063336153630011728/media/2063335199073533952)
On every PR that touches your skills directory, only the changed skills are scanned, fast, deterministic, no API keys needed in --no-llm mode. The scan posts a Markdown report directly on the PR, uploads SARIF to the Security tab, and blocks the merge if any skill scores above 50\. A separate weekly workflow scans the full registry for ongoing visibility but never blocks. The gate only lives on PRs.
Seen in practice: Claude Code Templates
Claude Code Templates (
[aitmpl.com](http://x.com/i/article/2063325372775575552//aitmpl.com)
) runs SkillSpector on every PR that adds or modifies a skill in the registry.
Check this PR:
<https://github.com/davila7/claude-code-templates/pull/623>
[!

item.content:encoded:
Iven ʕ•̬͡•ʔ✧ (@ivenvd)

看到 Hacker News 上有人表达跟我一样的观点了，并且推荐 Scoped Commits。 https://sumnerevans.com/posts/software-engineering/stop-using-conventional-commits/

🔗 Stop Using Conventional Commits - Sumner Evans

Posted
on
in
[Software Engineering](https://sumnerevans.com/categories/software-engineering)
• 1882 words
• 9 minute read
Tags:
[Git](https://sumnerevans.com/tags/git), [Commits](https://sumnerevans.com/tags/commits), [Scoped Commits](https://sumnerevans.com/tags/scoped-commits), [Conventional Commits](https://sumnerevans.com/tags/conventional-commits)
You’ve almost certainly encountered
[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) before.
It may have reared its ugly head in the changelog of an open source project
you’ve used. It may have been the enforced commit format for an open source
project you contributed to. A lot of people swear by it. I swear at it.
Even though it is used by
[a](https://github.com/angular/angular/blob/main/contributing-docs/commit-message-guidelines.md)
[large](https://electronjs.org/docs/development/pull-requests#commit-message-guidelines)
[number](https://contribute.freecodecamp.org/how-to-contribute-to-the-codebase/)
[of](https://jenkins-x.io/community/code/)
[popular](https://github.com/conventional-changelog/commitlint/blob/master/.github/CONTRIBUTING.md)
[open](https://github.com/semantic-release/semantic-release/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
[source](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md)
[projects](https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/main/.github/commit-convention.md),
Conventional Commits is an actively bad standard which
[encourages focus on the wrong things](https://sumnerevans.com#focus-failure) and
[fails to deliver on its promises](https://sumnerevans.com#broken-promises).
Focus Failure
Conventional Commits promises to add semantic meaning to commit messages to aid
developers and end-users in understanding the changes made in a commit. However,
Conventional Commits fails to do this in spectacular fashion. To demonstrate
this, let’s look at the anatomy of a conventional commit. According to the
[Conventional Commit website](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/#summary)
commit messages should be formatted as follows:
<type>[optional scope]: <description>
[optional body]
[optional footer(s)]
The commit’s subject line has a <type>
(something like fix
, feat
, chore
,
docs
, or refactor
[1](https://sumnerevans.com#fn:1)) describing the type of change. Following that, there
is an optional scope, and then a description.
This format has a major failing: type is prioritised over scope. This is exactly backwards.
Scope > Type
The scope of a change (the subject of the change) is the most important part of a commit. To demonstrate this, let’s consider why each one of the following stakeholders care about the scope of the change more than the type of the change:
Contributors: when you are a contributor to a project, you often need to read the commit log to identify changes in the codebase relevant to a certain area of the code. There are many reasons for this including:
- Wanting to catch up on what has happened since the last time you contributed.
- Trying to understand where the project’s overall inertia is.
- Looking for commits that might conflict with your in-progress work when pulling or rebasing.
As you read the commit log, you’re looking at what areas were touched. You really do not care about the type of change happening, you care about the scope of the change.
Debuggers: when investigating a bug, you often want to look through the commit log to see what changes might have touched areas related to the component where the bug manifested. Once again, the scope is the most important piece of information. The type of change is entirely useless because bugs can be introduced in any change regardless of type. (I’m sure we’ve all experienced writing a bugfix that caused another bug.)
Incident responders: when production is down, scanning the commit log for changes that were made around the time of the outage is an effective way to identify what areas may be causing the problem. Scope is once again the most important piece of information you can h

item.content:encoded:
nisedo (@nisedo_)

A must read

https://www.0xkato.xyz/how-llms-actually-work/

🔗 How LLMs Actually Work | 0xkato

How LLMs Actually Work
- 26 minsThis post is a walkthrough of how LLMs work. Modern LLMs are mostly built by stacking transformer blocks over and over, so understanding the transformer machinery gets you most of the way there.
I’ll cover the core mechanisms inside modern transformer-based LLMs, without all that sticky math stuff. Don’t get me wrong, you should learn the math, but this can serve as an introduction.
Most modern LLMs share the same transformer-family skeleton. The differences come from what each one was trained on, the scale and configuration choices, and the post-training done on top. By the end, you should be able to read many modern LLM papers or model cards and know which piece of the architecture each section is talking about.
Here’s the path:
- Tokens, how a string of text becomes a sequence of integers
- Embeddings, how those integers get meaning
- Positional encoding, how the model knows what order the tokens came in
- Attention, how tokens share information with each other
- Multi-head attention, how the model tracks many kinds of relationships at once
- The feed-forward network, where a large share of the model’s stored structure lives
- The residual stream and layer normalization, what makes deep stacks trainable
- Predicting the next token, what the model actually outputs and how the generation loop works
- Architecture vs trained weights, what’s broadly shared across modern LLMs, and what’s different
Tiny explainers appear throughout so anyone can follow along, regardless of background.
Tokenization
Models don’t read text directly. They read integer IDs. The step that converts your prompt into a sequence of those integers.
That conversion step is called tokenization. A tokenizer takes a string and produces a sequence of integers, where each integer points to an entry in a fixed vocabulary. Modern LLM vocabularies usually contain tens of thousands to a few hundred thousand entries.
Tiny explainer: token ID
A token ID is the integer the model uses for one vocabulary entry. The model works with the number, not the written word itself.
Tokens aren’t usually whole words. They’re usually subword pieces. The word “tokenization” might split into [“token”, “ization”]. The word “running” might split into [“run”, “ning”]. The reason is efficiency. Whole-word vocabularies are too big and don’t generalize to new words. Character-level vocabularies are too small and force the model to learn even the simplest patterns from scratch. Subword tokenization sits in the middle. The most common pieces become single tokens, and rare or novel words get composed from smaller pieces.
Tiny explainer: vocabulary
The vocabulary is the tokenizer’s fixed list of pieces. Each piece has an ID, and the model can only directly receive IDs from that list.
The trade-off shows up in places people don’t expect. The classic example: ask an LLM how many R’s are in “strawberry.” LLMs used to get it wrong. That’s not the model failing at counting. It’s the model not operating on letters directly, only token IDs that happen to spell out a word a human would split letter by letter.
Different model families use different tokenizers. GPT models use Byte Pair Encoding variants. SentencePiece is common in LLaMA-style models. The choice matters for compute (fewer tokens means less work) and for things like multilingual coverage, but the basic shape is the same. Text in, integers out.
Now that the prompt is a sequence of integers, the next step is to give those integers meaning.
Embeddings
A token ID like 1024
is just a row index. It doesn’t mean anything by itself. The thing that gives it meaning is a giant table called the embedding matrix.
Every model has one. It has one row per entry in the vocabulary, and each row is a long vector of numbers. The length of each row is the model’s hidden size. In many 7B-class models, that means 4,096 numbers per token. Larger models usually use wider vectors.
Tiny explainer: vector
A vector is a list of numbers.

i want to walk through an actual business idea here, the whole thing end to end, because i think it's one of the best opportunities sitting in front of anyone right now and barely anyone is running it properly.
the core of it is this. there are millions of ordinary businesses out there, quietly drowning in manual work. and the money in that isn't in walking up and selling them ai, because that almost never works. the second you say the words ai or automation to a guy who runs, let's say a concrete company, he stops hearing you, because those words mean nothing to him except expensive and risky and probably going to break the thing he spent his whole life building.
so you don't sell him the automation. you sell him something tiny and obvious first, something he can see the value immediately, and you let that little thing get you in the door.
the tool i'd lead with is dead simple. the owner drops in his website, it pulls his logo and his colours and the photos he's already got sitting there, and it hands him thirty social media posts in his own branding, ready to put up for the month. that's the whole thing. you charge him $99/mo and he says yes without really thinking about it, because he already knows he's supposed to be posting every day, and $99/mo is nothing to him. he's holding the result in his hand and there's nothing to explain to him.
but that was never the point. that tool is a door, and the only thing that actually matters is what's on the other side of it, which is that this man now pays you every month, opens your thing every week.that's trust, sitting right in front of the exact kind of owner who would have ignored your email a month ago. and you can build that with a few hundred of them at the same time, because the tool just runs on its own.
then one day you get him on a call, and you're not selling him anything, you just ask how the business is going, and he starts telling you about the stuff that's actually grinding him down. it's never the exciting stuff. it's quotes he puts together manually, invoices he types in one at a time, leads that die because nobody chased them etc., i had a client whose entire company was basically running out of one enormous broken spreadsheet, and we built them something that pulled their invoices straight off their site and dropped them into one clean dashboard on their own. that mess was costing him hours every week and real money on top of it, far more than the little tool ever was, and now you're the obvious person to fix it, because you've already proven you can be trusted with a piece of how he makes his living.
so you build him the real thing. if his problem is big you build one proper system for it, usually a dashboard/agent that plugs straight into the crm he's already using so everything finally lives in one place. if it's smaller you build two or three automations that just does the boring work for him. either way you're charging at least $5000/mo to run it.

The Backpressure Loop Pattern for Coding Agents
[![](https://pbs.twimg.com/profile_images/1779610675431591936/WMVtJ651_normal.jpg)](http://x.com/i/article/2060705098053890053/bibryam)

Coding agents made code generation faster. They did not make code validation faster. >>That is the bottleneck <<
Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and similar tools can now produce useful diffs quickly. But when the agent works without feedback, the human becomes the first real quality gate.
✗ The human checks the build.
✗ The human finds the broken test.
✗ The human notices the missing import.
✗ The human spots the visual bug.
✗ The human explains the issue and sends the agent back for another try.
✗ That is not review.
✗ That is babysitting.
The pattern that fixes this is the Backpressure Loop.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKJ6oejXQAAZWYp?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2060705098053890053/bibryam/article/2063349737089331531/media/2063346415103852544)
Backpressure is feedback that reaches the agent before the agent reaches the human.
The source can be a type checker, test, linter, build, browser check, log, trace, structural rule, or eval. The important part is the loop:
agent changes code → system pushes back → agent repairs → agent retries.
##
1\. Move feedback into the agent loop
✓ A coding agent is a fast producer.
✗ A human reviewer is a slow consumer.
When all meaningful feedback comes from the human, every simple failure becomes review work. That does not scale.
The goal is not only to ask:
How good is the model?
The better question is:
What feedback can the agent use without asking me?
If the agent can run the type checker, read the failure, fix the code, and try again, the human should not be involved yet.
The human should review intent, design, trade-offs, and product behavior.
The system should catch mechanical failures first.
##
2\. CI is not enough
A CI failure after the agent is finished is a gate.
A failure the agent sees while working is backpressure.
That distinction matters.
A green build is useful, but narrow. It tells you the code compiled, formatted, and passed existing tests. It does not prove the product rule survived. It does not prove the generated test asserts meaningful behavior. It does not prove the refactor respected the architecture.
So the goal is not just “run CI earlier.”
The goal is to make feedback fast, specific, and actionable enough for the agent to repair the work.
✗ Bad feedback:
> The code is wrong.
✓ Better feedback:
> auth/session.test.ts failed. Expected expired sessions to redirect to /login. Received 200 from /dashboard. Fix the session expiration path. Do not change the test.
The second version gives the agent something to do.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKJ7HXRXgAA0Mdk?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/i/article/2060705098053890053/bibryam/article/2063349737089331531/media/2063346945725267968)
##
3\. Compress success, expand failure
More output is not better feedback.
A thousand lines of passing logs can be worse than a short signal.
Useful backpressure should be:
* informative
* valid
* non-redundant
* retained for the next attempt
Passing checks should be tiny.
Failing checks should be actionable.
Example:
✓ typecheck ✓ lint ✗ auth tests FAIL auth/session.test.ts Expected redirect to /login for expired sessi
